vignette:
Rodrigo is a 67-year-old widowed Latin American man who has spent nearly four decades as a prosecutor in a mid-sized American city. He came to his first intake session dressed with careful formality - a pressed shirt, a tie he straightened twice before sitting down - and he spoke with the measured precision of a man accustomed to constructing narratives for courtrooms. What he had not been able to construct, he admitted quietly, was any account of the past fourteen months that made sense to him.

The assault occurred at a professional conference held at a hotel in another city. A colleague he had known for over a decade - a man he had shared meals with, testified alongside, trusted in the way that professionals trust those who have stood beside them in difficult work - followed Rodrigo to his hotel room after a late dinner and forced himself on him. Rodrigo remembered the specific weight of the man's hands, the temperature of the room, which had been kept cold by the air conditioning, a chill he had noticed absently when he first entered and that had settled against his skin throughout. He had not fought back in the way he later felt he should have. He had frozen. For a man who had spent his career demanding accountability in courtrooms, this felt, in some part of himself he could not silence, like a verdict against him.

In the weeks that followed, Rodrigo returned to work. He told no one. He filed nothing. He was aware, with a prosecutor's clarity, of the irony, and it shamed him further. The memory did not behave as he expected memories to behave - it did not recede with time but instead arrived without warning, fully formed and insistent, as though the event were still in progress rather than finished. He would be reading a brief at his desk when the memory would force its way in, not as recollection but as presence, and he would find himself back in that cold room, the details vivid and undiminished. He had come to feel that his mind was no longer reliably his own.

Certain things became unbearable without his fully understanding why they had. The cold air from the courthouse's aging ventilation system, which he had never previously noticed, began to register against his skin as a specific, recognisable sensation that tightened something in his chest. He started requesting to work in conference rooms on the building's south side, where the heating was better, and his colleagues attributed this to the eccentricities of age. When he appeared in court and found himself in the presence of children - a victim's family, a custody case, a juvenile proceeding - he felt a distress he could not articulate and began quietly reassigning those cases to junior staff. When he encountered any of the colleagues who had attended that conference, even peripherally, he would leave the room.

He had stopped going to unfamiliar restaurants, unfamiliar buildings, anywhere he could not anticipate the layout. In every room he entered - his own office included - he found himself marking the exits, noting what was near at hand that could be used as a weapon or that someone else might use. He understood, in the rational part of his mind, that these habits were disproportionate, but what frightened him most was that they did not feel disproportionate. They felt like the only reasonable response to a world he now understood to be genuinely dangerous in ways he had previously underestimated. He had come to believe that his prior sense of safety had been a form of ignorance, and that the assault had simply revealed what had always been true.

He had also come to feel that something in his body had been permanently altered - not in any way he could name to a physician, but in the way he inhabited himself, the way he moved through space. He felt contaminated in a manner that had not lifted with time or with the showers he took each morning, which had grown longer and more effortful without resolving anything. He had not been intimate with anyone since his wife's death three years prior, and he was now certain he never would be, though he did not examine that certainty closely.

What finally brought him to seek help was a meeting with a young victim of assault - a case he could not reassign - during which he had sat across from her and understood, with sudden and unwelcome clarity, that he recognised exactly what she was describing. He arrived at his first session hoping, above all else, to be able to do his job again. What he feared most was being asked to say aloud what had happened to him.
